Look for herald patch preceding elliptical rash along Langer lines. C
Pityriasis rosea is distinguished by a collarette of scale just inside the erythematous border of the patch. A collarette scale is paper-thin scale with central clearing. C

background.definition: Pityriasis rosea (PR) is a common, usually asymptomatic, self-limited, papulosquamous skin disorder lasting 2 to 12 weeks and presents as 5 to 15 mm, mildly erythematous, salmon-colored, elliptically-shaped patches and plaques with fine collarette of scale. Lesions occur in a characteristic "Christmas tree" pattern, with the long axis of the ellipse following cleavage (Langer) lines of the trunk; sparing of the palms, soles, and face is typical. The first visible lesion, the so-called "herald patch," is a 2 to 10 cm, solitary, flesh-colored or pink patch or plaque with scale, usually found on the trunk, and precedes the generalized eruption by up to 2 weeks.

list.listitem: Varies according to series.
Most common in adolescents and young adults, with peak age between 15 and 30 years.
172.2 cases per 100,000 person-years, based on a 10-year study in Minnesota in the 1970s.
It represents 0.3% to 1.2% of patients diagnosed by dermatologists worldwide.
There is conflicting data on seasonal variation especially based on geography, but incidence appears highest during cold months.
Unclear etiology, but likely infectious.

Possibly viral, because of clustering of cases, association with concomitant or preceeding viral prodrome, lack of recurrence suggesting presence of prolonged immunity, and associated inflammatory markers (e.g., elevated sedimentation rate, B-cell increase, TH1-cell decrease, and reduction in IFN gamma). Systemic reactivation of human herpesvirus (HHV)-6 and HHV-7 has been suggested as the cause, but other studies have not demonstrated this association.
Pityriasis rosea like eruptions have been reported following COVID-19 vaccination.
Likely not associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1 and HSV-2, Mycoplasma, Legionella, or Chlamydia, based on laboratory studies.
Unknown.
Histology may show acute and chronic inflammatory change with dyskeratotic degeneration in epidermis.
Typically presents with salmon-colored, 5 to 15 mm, elliptical patches and plaques following cleavage lines in mainly truncal distribution (). C

Patients may report a history of a "herald patch" (), a 2 to 10 cm patch preceding the rest of the rash and distinguished by a collarette of scale just inside the erythematous border of the patch (). C
Consider secondary syphilis, atopic dermatitis, and tinea in selected patients at risk for syphilis or with prolonged or severe symptoms. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pityriasis may, but usually does not, affect palms and soles: check RPR or TPA (treponema pallidum antibody) if indicated. Check rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or treponema pallidum antibody (TPA)
Classic AD is flexural in distribution, whereas pityriasis shows Christmas tree pattern
Skin scraping using a KOH prep may help rule out tinea
Does not follow Langer lines; collarette pattern absent; scale usually thicker and more prominent
Eczema responds readily to topical corticosteroids; a history of eczema, allergies, or asthma may be present
Tinea has an advancing border and KOH prep shows hyphae
Exposure to drug precedes rash and discontinuation causes resolution; intense pruritus; absence of herald patch, fine collarette of scale, and Christmas tree pattern

list.listitem: Mild prodromal illness is seen in about 70% of patients. Age range of 9 months to 82 years, although 87% of cases occur between the ages of 10 and 39 years.

Typical presentation consists of a larger (2-10 cm) "herald patch" preceding appearance of a generalized rash by up to two weeks, followed by salmon-colored elliptical papules, plaques, and patches of 5 to 15 mm, with long axis following skin lines. There is typically a slight scale or "collarette" of scale just inside the erythematous border. The rash is usually asymptomatic or associated with mild pruritus only.
If rash is on back, look for typical "Christmas tree" distribution, with lesions slanting upward along Langer lines, suggestive of the "spine-like branches of an evergreen."

Diagnosis may be difficult in a minority of patients with atypical presentation, where the rash may be localized (instead of generalized) or may present in a non-classic distribution or morphology (e.g., pustular or vesicular).

PR-like eruptions are caused by medications or vaccines, and may resemble classic PR. They have been reported in patients using angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), thiazide diuretics, allopurinol, aspirin, gold compounds, bismuth, and other medications. Use of kinase inhibitors, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, and other biologics have also been implicated, but it is unclear whether they cause classic PR (by way of systemic reactivation of HHV-6/7 secondary to immune-suppression) or PR-like cutaneous drug eruption. PR-like eruptions due to vaccines have been associated with Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG), hepatitis B, influenza (H1N1), human papillomavirus (HPV), pneumococcal polysaccharide, smallpox, and yellow fever vaccines.
Additional testing and workup is usually not indicated (see Differential Diagnosis).
None, unless the patient has a history putting him/her at risk for syphilis. If so, consider RPR on blood, fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA) or darkfield of lesion, or TPA on blood.
Consider scraping and KOH prep or fungal culture to rule out tinea if symptoms persist.
A recent study examined dermoscopy, and found that pityriasis rosea is characterized by a yellowish background, peripheral scales, and dotted vessels.

Some experts suggest that identification of HHV-6/7 DNA in plasma or IgM antibiodies in serum is suggestive of classic PR, while peripheral eosinophilia and dermal eosinophils (on biopsy) are supportive of PR-like eruption.
Diagnosis is clinical. Look for typical lesions along Langer lines and elicit history of herald patch.
Consider evaluation for secondary syphilis, tinea, psoriasis, PR-like drug eruption, and atopic dermatitis in selected patients.
Treatment is not necessary in most cases. C
Topical steroids, topical antipruritics, or oral antihistamines may help with pruritus. C
Systemic steroids may help pruritus and improve rash, but risks should be weighed against benefits. C
Acyclovir may hasten clinician-rated resolution of rash, but has uncertain effects on pruritus. A
Erythromycin may reduce pruritus. A
Withdraw any drug that may be causing PR-like eruption. C

Treatment is not necessary in most cases, especially when pruritus is not prominent. A topical steroid or topical antipruritic (e.g., calamine lotion) may be beneficial for localized itching. Oral diphenhydramine or hydroxyzine can be considered for generalized pruritus.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 70 adult patients compared tapering prednisolone doses over 2 weeks with placebo. The improvement in pruritus score and objective rash score were better in the prednisolone group with no adverse events in either group. The relapse rate at 12 weeks was much higher in the prednisolone group. Oral steroids may be considered in extensive and highly symptomatic disease.

A 2019 Cochrane Review found moderate-quality evidence based on 3 studies with 141 participants that acyclovir improves clinician-rated rash score better than all comparators (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.33 to 4.53). Placebo may be better than acyclovir for itch resolution based on 1 study with 21 patients (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.94), but itch score reduction was not studied. No serious adverse events were reported in either group, and minor side effects were similar between groups.

The same systematic review found moderate-quality evidence based on 1 study with 34 patients that erythromycin decreases itch score better than placebo (MD 3.95, 95% CI 3.37 to 4.53). No serious adverse events occurred, and minor adverse events were similar between groups. In contrast, the authors concluded that azithromycin appears no better than placebo in decreasing pruritus and improving rash.

Based on 2 trials of 17 and 100 patients, ultraviolet (UV) B phototherapy may improve disease severity and symptoms compared to placebo. A trial enrolling 15 patients with extensive disease found UVA phototherapy improves disease severity and pruritus. More rigorous trials are needed before phototherapy can be routinely recommended; adverse events need to be studied thoroughly.
Rash and symptoms usually resolve in 2 to 12 weeks with or without treatment. C
Serious sequelae are rare. C

A case series from Italy of 38 pregnant women diagnosed with PR noted 9 premature deliveries and 5 spontaneous abortions. Specifically, 62% had spontaneous abortion when PR occurred during the first 15 weeks of pregnancy. HHV-6 was implicated in 1 closely studied patient.

Another series of 33 pregnant women with pityriasis rosea during pregnancy found 8 birth complications including nuchal cord, meconium passage, small for gestational age, preterm birth, and fetal distress. Rates of preterm birth, oligohydramnios and spontanous pregnancy loss were similar to that seen in the general population. This included 18 women with PR before 15 weeks gestation, who had 5 birth complications.
Some authors recommend consideration of acyclovir to treat PR in early pregnancy, but strong evidence to support this recommendation is lacking.
Similarly, evidence to support treatment of PR in breastfeeding women using acyclovir is lacking.
Clinical presentation of PR in children is similar to adults, but pruritus may be more common in children.

African-American children may have more scalp (8%) and facial involvement (30%) compared to Caucasian children. Post-inflammatory dyspigmentation is common (48% hyperpigmentation; 29% hypopigmentation when lesions are papular or papulovesicular). Rash resolves within 2 weeks in about 50% of black children.
There is insufficient evidence to treat PR in children using acyclovir.
